description_ru: Как вакцины обучают иммунную систему, от опыта Дженнера до современных мРНК-вакцин и коллективного иммунитета.
text:
Every day, your body is attacked by millions of microscopic invaders. Most of them are defeated so quickly that you never notice. But some diseases, such as measles, polio and smallpox, are dangerous because they spread fast and can cause serious damage before the body has time to respond. Vaccines have been designed to solve exactly this problem. They teach the immune system how to recognise a dangerous germ without making you ill, so that when the real germ arrives, your body is already prepared.

The idea is much older than modern science. In 1796, an English doctor named Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught a mild disease called cowpox seemed to be protected from smallpox, which killed and scarred millions of people. He took some fluid from a cowpox sore and put it into a small cut on the arm of a young boy. When he later exposed the boy to smallpox, the boy did not become sick. The word "vaccine" actually comes from the Latin word for cow, vacca. Nearly two hundred years later, in 1980, the World Health Organization announced that smallpox had been completely eradicated.

To understand how a vaccine works, it helps to know a little about the immune system. Your body is full of white blood cells, which patrol the blood and tissues. Every germ carries molecules on its surface called antigens. When white blood cells detect an unfamiliar antigen, they begin to produce proteins called antibodies, which attach to the invader and mark it for destruction. However, making the right antibodies for a new germ can take several days. During that time, the germ multiplies, and the person may become seriously ill.

A vaccine gives the body a safe preview. It contains a harmless piece or version of a germ, and this is enough to start the immune response. The white blood cells recognise the antigen, produce antibodies and, most importantly, create special memory cells. These cells can survive for years, sometimes for a whole lifetime. If the real germ ever enters the body, the memory cells recognise it immediately and release a large number of antibodies within hours, instead of days. In many cases, the person has no symptoms at all.

There are several different kinds of vaccine. Some contain a weakened form of the living germ, which cannot cause the disease in healthy people but still looks familiar to the immune system. The vaccines against measles and chickenpox are made this way. Others contain a germ that has been killed, or only a small part of it, such as a single protein. A more recent type, called an mRNA vaccine, does not contain any part of the germ at all. Instead, it carries a short set of instructions that tells your cells to make one harmless protein, and the immune system learns to recognise it. The instructions are destroyed by the body within a few days.

Why do some vaccines need more than one dose? The answer is that a single introduction is often not enough to create a strong, long-lasting memory. A second dose, called a booster, reminds the immune system and makes the response stronger. Other vaccines, such as the one for influenza, need to be repeated every year, because the flu virus changes quickly. Scientists must predict which versions will be common each winter and adjust the vaccine accordingly, which is why it is not perfect, although it still reduces serious illness.

Vaccines protect not only the person who receives them, but also the people around them. If most of a community is immune, the germ cannot move easily from one person to another, and it eventually disappears. This effect is known as herd immunity. It is especially important for babies who are too young to be vaccinated, and for people with weak immune systems. For measles, which is extremely contagious, about ninety-five percent of the population need to be vaccinated before the community is properly protected.

Like any medicine, vaccines can cause side effects. Most are mild and short: a sore arm, a slight fever or tiredness for a day or two. These are signs that the immune system is working. Serious reactions are extremely rare, and before a vaccine is approved, it is tested on thousands of volunteers and monitored for years. If doctors had not been so careful, many people would have lost their trust, and diseases that are now uncommon would have returned.

Today, vaccines prevent several million deaths every year, according to the World Health Organization. Researchers are working on new ones against malaria, which kills hundreds of thousands of children annually, and even against some kinds of cancer. Whenever you roll up your sleeve for an injection, you are taking part in one of the greatest achievements in medical history, a science that began with a country doctor, a few milkmaids and a very brave boy.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Верхние зубы касаются нижней губы, звук звонкий; не превращайте его в «в» с округлением губ.
Кончик языка слегка между зубами, выдыхайте мягко; не заменяйте на «с» или «з».
Начните с «э» и плавно скользите к «и»; не обрывайте звук.
Выделяйте ударный слог длиннее и громче, остальные слоги редуцируйте.

questions.question: Who tested the first vaccine, and when?
questions.answer: Edward Jenner in 1796, using cowpox against smallpox.

questions.question: What are memory cells?
questions.answer: Cells that remember a germ and react quickly if it returns.

questions.question: What is herd immunity?
questions.answer: When most people are immune, a germ cannot spread easily.

questions.question: What side effects are usual after vaccination?
questions.answer: A sore arm, a slight fever or tiredness.
